analysis.one_liner: Exempts livestock manure from Superfund toxic-substance rules and emergency release reporting.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 30 senators from both parties, was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal toxic-substance law so that livestock manure — including the chemicals and process water mixed with it — no longer counts as a hazardous substance under Superfund (CERCLA), the law that lets the government and citizens force cleanup of contaminated sites. It would also have exempted manure-related releases from the emergency notification rules that require facilities to tell communities and officials when toxic gases are released. In practice, this would have shielded large animal feeding operations from Superfund cleanup lawsuits and from having to report ammonia and hydrogen sulfide air releases to nearby residents.
analysis.who_benefits: Large livestock, poultry, and dairy operations (concentrated animal feeding operations) would have gained the most: they could not be sued under Superfund to pay for cleaning up manure contamination, and they would no longer have to report manure-related air releases under emergency planning laws. Smaller family farms that handle manure would also have been protected from liability, which is how supporters framed the bill.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defined 'manure' broadly to include not just animal waste but bedding, compost, process water, and any byproduct or emission from those materials, then removed all of it from the definitions of 'hazardous substance' and 'pollutant or contaminant' under CERCLA [S3].

It amended the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act so that manure-related releases were exempt from the emergency notification requirements that otherwise force facilities to alert communities and state officials about toxic releases [S2][S3].

The bill said it would not affect other environmental laws or an existing EPA Air Quality Agreement with animal feeding operations, which supporters could point to as evidence that other protections remained in place [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living near large animal feeding operations would have lost the ability to learn about ammonia and hydrogen sulfide releases next door and lost a legal path to force cleanup of manure-contaminated land and water under Superfund. Taxpayers would have been more likely to foot cleanup costs that industry would otherwise pay.

drawbacks.text: Residents near large feeding operations would have lost the right-to-know protections under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-To-Know Act, since the bill specifically provided it would not impose any manure-related liability under that law [S3].

Superfund cleanup claims against farms for manure contamination would have ended, meaning communities and governments could no longer use that law to make operators pay for contaminated sites [S2][S3].

The bill's own carve-outs — other environmental laws still apply, and an existing EPA air agreement remains in force — would have left its practical protection narrower than its broad liability exemption, but the loss of release reporting and cleanup liability was real [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered genuine liability relief that smaller farms could value, but its broadly written manure definition swept in the largest concentrated animal operations and removed two tools that neighbors rely on: knowing what is being released into their air and forcing cleanup of contaminated sites. The industry shield was much larger than the family-farm benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Blanche Lincoln introduced the bill with eight co-introducers on March 8, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The bill picked up 29 cosponsors — 26 Republicans and 3 Democrats — but the committee took no further action on it [S4][S5].
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People living near large livestock operations kept the existing Superfund and community right-to-know protections the bill would have removed, and large livestock operators remained exposed to the same cleanup liability as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rural residents near large livestock operations

for.name: Sen. Blanche Lincoln
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt manure from Superfund and emergency release reporting rules.

for.name: 26 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, providing most of its support.

for.name: 3 of 51 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Pryor of Arkansas.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — after the bill was referred, letting it die.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: a Democrat from Arkansas led the bill and 26 of its 29 cosponsors were Republicans, but no vote was ever taken so the issue never split the chamber.

industries.industry: Large livestock and poultry operations (concentrated animal feeding operations)
industries.note: The bill would have freed these operations from Superfund cleanup liability and from reporting manure-related ammonia and hydrogen sulfide releases, shifting those costs and risks onto neighboring communities and potentially taxpayers. The exemption's broad definition of manure covered industrial-scale operations, not just family farms.
